newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO begin new year without Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO begin new year without Hebron deal.

text.p: Israelis and Palestinians greeted the new year still a step away from agreement on an Israeli withdrawal from the key West Bank town of Hebron.

Negotiators finalised most parts of a deal which would finally give Palestinians self-rule in Hebron, but outstanding disputes prevented U.S. envoy Dennis Ross arranging a summit between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

"We're still working and I think there is a genuine desire to reach an agreement. So we are going to keep working and I hope we can reach it soon," Ross told reporters after meeting Arafat in Gaza on Tuesday.
Asked if a meeting could take place on Thursday, Ross said: "What I prefer to do is to keep working and we'll see. When we get there, we get there."

Israeli and PLO officials had said earlier the leaders would probably meet on Wednesay as negotiators had ironed out most issues. But the two sides were still at odds over future withdrawals and the release of Palestinian prisoners.
"There are still some outstanding issues which need to be resolved," said chief Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat on Tuesday.
The deal would set in motion Israel's withdrawal from 80 percent of Hebron -- a flashpoint of violence between Arabs and Jews -- nine months after the due date for the redeployment.
Netanyahu's demand for security measures to protect around 400 Jewish settlers in the town has held up the Israeli pullout outlined in a 1995 Israel-PLO peace deal.

"The agreement on Hebron has been concluded. The problem is what comes after Hebron. We are still discussing other outstanding issues such as further redeployments and prisoners," said Major-General Abdel-Razak al-Yahya, a top negotiator.
The PLO wants Israel to free Palestinian prisoners as part of the deal, viewing a release as crucial to winning support for peace deals on the Palestinian street.
Hebron is the last town due to get self-rule but West Bank rural areas remain on the agenda. Officials have said the Hebron redeployment could take place within hours of any deal.
Jewish settlers in the town said they were praying for a miracle to prevent Israeli troops from pulling back and warned of impending bloodshed.
Settlers scuffled with Palestinians near a Jewish enclave in the town on Tuesday and tried to take over Arab houses in the casbah.
Israeli security forces made 15 arrests, said the settlers, who oppose a handover of any part of the town holy to Moslems and Jews as the burial place of the Abraham.

"There are military intelligence documents that have revealed Arafat is planning on filling those homes with 600 terrorists...released from Israeli jails," said David Wilder, a spokesman for the Jews in Hebron.
Jewish settlers, who number 130,000 in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, helped Netanyahu sweep to power in elections last May on a promise to be tough with the Palestinians.

But the right-wing Netanyahu has come under pressure from Washington, Israel's closest ally, to honour peace deals reached during the term of the previous left-leaning government and withdraw from Hebron.
In a message delivered by Ross, President Bill Clinton praised Netanyahu for "decisions which the prime minister made in order to advance the peace talks" and invited him to Washington.
